doc.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Etudes, tension and release, and silence in music
summary: Etudes are not music; good music is tension and release, with silence important; musicianship cannot be taught, only encouraged.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: No, they’re etudes. And etudes are studies and that’s what they were meant to be, and that’s what they are. Because you can’t consider most etudes as music, because they’re not. You know they were designed to do a certain thing. Technically you know. But you know most students, they spend so much time doing that that when they come out and start playing they think they’re making music when it’s got nothing to do with that. It’s two different things. I can be the greatest saxophone player in the world and not be able to make a note of music. It’s two different things. See so they have to get, they almost have to forget that.

And forget it. And then make some music, you know what I mean? Because it’s been my observation that all good music, regardless of what type it is, European music or I don’t care, any kind of music, it’s all a matter of, well it’s an extension actually of us. And we, as a part of the universe, we operate the same way. It’s a matter of tension and release. And in music it’s the same thing, you see what I mean? And in the best music, I’ve noticed it’s the artful use of that tension and release that makes the music, using the components of music which are first rhythm, because you can have rhythm without melody, and melody and harmony, and the one that’s ignored so much — which is this is important — is silence. Because that is the ultimate release to sound. And it’s the silence that makes the sound important. So if you keep on playing, it gets to be more and more meaningless as you go. So you have to—
I guess Basie was a good example of that.

Oh, yeah, well it’s a matter of communicating as opposed to self gratification, you know, which is not nice in public. So kids, you know, they gradually grow out of that, but some of them naturally understand that, but I mean there are some, quite a few that don’t. They’re so wrapped up in playing the instrument and the patterns and all the things that they’ve learned and trying to get out there, you know what I mean, they forget about they’re supposed to be making music and communicating, which is an entirely different thing. Some cats could do more with, like our old cats, they didn’t have, they didn’t use all the complex harmonies that we use today. They’d build a better house with just a hammer and a nail than you did with all the electric saws and stuff. So it’s a matter of making music. It’s got nothing to do with all that other stuff. So that’s what students should really think about you know.
That’s the hardest thing to teach too.

You know you can’t teach that, music is, well the only thing you can do, somebody that has potential, you just have to make them aware of that. You can’t teach them that. You © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
make them aware of that and then they handle it in their way. You can’t teach anybody that. You can put it there, but as far as teaching it, that’s another thing.
You can coach but you can’t—
I think it has a lot to do with how much they’ve listened to as they grow up and their experience too.
